notes.text: On this wise — Hebrew. Thus, or in these words: yet they were not tied to these very words; because after this we have examples of Moses and David and Solomon, blessing the people in other words.

Bless thee — Bestow upon you all manner of blessings, temporal and spiritual. Keep thee - That is, continue his blessings to thee, and preserve thee in and to the use of them; keep thee from sin and its bitter effects.

Shine upon thee — Alluding to the shining of the sun upon the earth, to enlighten, and warm, and renew the face of it. The Lord love thee, and make thee know that he loves thee. We cannot but be happy, if we have God's love; and we cannot but be easy, if we know that we have it.

Lift up his countenance — That is, look upon thee with a chearful and pleasant countenance, as one that is well pleased with thee and thy services. Peace - Peace with God, with thy own conscience, and with all men; all prosperity is comprehended under this word.

Put my name — Shall call them by my name, shall recommend them to me as my own people, and bless them and pray unto me for them as such; which is a powerful argument to prevail with God for them. The offerings of the princes upon the dedication of the tabernacle, ver. 1-9. Upon the dedication of the altar, ver. 10-88, Which God graciously accepts, ver. 89.

glossa.text:
*And he spoke.* Moses signifies the law, Aaron the priesthood, and his sons the order of the Church. The Lord therefore teaches through the law the order of the priests, how they may build up the people by preaching, and confirm them by frequent prayer and blessing.

((RAB., ubi supra. )) Moses has a manifold signification, etc., *as far as* while he completes, raises and anoints the tabernacle.

*May he bless.* ((ID.)) It is to be noted that in this blessing the name of the Lord is brought in three times, that the holy Trinity may be understood, from whom and through whom and in whom all good things are to be sought and obtained, because of him and through him and in him are all things.

*And may he keep.* ((ID.)) May he preserve by his grace the blessing which thou hast received: *Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it ((Psal. CXXVI))*.
*May he show.* The showing of the face of God is propitiation, and the showing of true salvation; whence: *Show thy face, and we shall be saved ((Psal. LXXVII))*.

*May he turn,* etc. The turning of the face signifies mercy, the turning away, wrath; whence: *Look upon me and have mercy on me ((Psal. CXVIII))*. And elsewhere: *Why turnest thou away thy face, and forgettest our want? ((Psal. XLIII.))* We must pray therefore that he whose help we turn away from us by sinning may through his own goodness vouchsafe to make his face shine upon us, so that, rescuing us from our enemies, he may grant perpetual peace.

*They shall invoke.* ((ID.)) It belongs to the priests to invoke the name of the Lord: but to the Lord, to accomplish what is asked. Let no one therefore ascribe to himself what the Trinity alone bestows on whom it wills.

notes.text: In — Not only in Israel, but among all nations. Which shews that this psalm speaks of the Messiah, and the times of the New Testament. Heavens - Where thy throne of glory is established, where the blessed angels celebrate thy praises, where Christ sitteth at thy right hand in glorious majesty, from whence he poureth down excellent gifts upon babes.

Babes — Weak and foolish, and contemptible persons, who are frequently called babes or children. Such are very unfit to grapple with an enemy: and therefore when such persons conquer the most powerful and malicious enemies, it must needs confound them, and advance the glory of God: as indeed it did, when such mean persons as the apostles, and disciples of Christ, maintained and propagated the gospel, in spite of all the wit, power, and rage of their enemies. Ordained - Perfectly or firmly settled strength; that is, the praise of his strength or power, Matt. xxi, 16, it is rendered praise. Still - Silence and confound them. Avenger - The devil, and all who are his vassals and espouse his quarrel.

The moon — Either the sun is included under this general title: or he omitted it, because he made this psalm by night. Ordained - Placed in that excellent and unalterable order, and directed to their several motions.

What is man — How mean and inconsiderable a thing is man, if compared with thy glorious majesty. Man - Hebrew. infirm, or miserable man. By which it is apparent that he speaks of man, not according to the state of his creation, but as fallen into a state of sin and misery, and mortality. Mindful - Carest for him, and conferest such high favours upon him. The son - Hebrew. the son of Adam, that great apostate from God, the sinful son of a sinful father, his son by likeness of disposition and manners, no less than by procreation. All which tends to magnify the following mercy. Visitest - Not in anger, as that word is sometimes used, but with thy grace and mercy.

For — Thou hast in Christ mercifully restored man to his primitive estate, wherein he was but one remove below the angels; from which he was fallen by sin. Crowned - Man, fallen and lost man: who is actually restored to glory and dominion in Christ his head and representative, who received this crown and dominion for man's good, and in his stead; which he will in due time communicate to his members. And so the two expositions of this place concerning mankind and concerning Christ, may be reconciled. For he speaks of that honourable estate conferred first upon Christ, and then by his hands upon mankind. But the words more literally rendered are, Thou madest him a little less than God. And hence some have inferred, that man in his original state was the highest of all creatures. David praises God for giving him victory over his enemies, ver. 1-6. Triumphs in confidence that God would judge the world and protect his people, ver. 7-10. Calls others to praise him, ver. 11, 12. Prays for help, and praises God, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician upon Muth-labben, A psalm of David Title of the psalm. Muth-labben - This also seems to be a title of some tune, or instrument: of which we may be content to be ignorant, as the Jewish doctors are.

glossa.text: « O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name! etc. » ((CASS.)) First the praises of God, his majesty, and his exalted working are described. « In the whole. » ((Ibid.)) Let not the Jews therefore, or any others, claim for themselves what belongs to all, which is the intent. « Above the heavens. » ((AUG.)) Literally, or the Scriptures: because it exceeds the utterances of all the Scriptures; or, « above the heavens. » Continuing with what follows, that is, into the Scriptures, which he bends down to babes, on account of the enemies of the cross: who are destroyed, when the Scriptures are seen, that is, understood, to be led down as far as babes: and when through them they are nourished unto strength, and are raised to the sublimity of understanding.

« Out of the mouth of infants. » ((Ibid.)) Of the unwise, to whom the Apostle gave milk, whom those signified who praised the Lord, in whom the Lord uses this testimony. Out of these he hath perfected praise, because if only the perfect were in the Church, no counsel would be taken for the human race; as now, when even the least, not yet capable of the knowledge of spiritual things, are nourished by faith in the history of things temporal. « Enemies » are all who speak things contrary to the dispensation made through the Crucified. « Defenders » the heretics seem of the faith, the philosophers of wisdom, although yet the former impugn the faith, and the latter true wisdom. « Sucklings, » ((CASS.)) not in age, but as Peter has it, « as newborn babes ((I Petr. II)), » who cannot yet take food, but milk; and it is: thou art proclaimed not only by the perfect, but also by the unwise. Or, he calls infants and sucklings the apostles, who were simple and unlearned men; whence: « The foolish things of the world « God hath chosen, that he may confound the strong ((I Cor. I)). » The praise is more perfect. Or, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, that is, out of the words of the Hebrew children thou hast perfected praise, which seemed to be done childishly, on account of the enemies, that it might not seem to be human wisdom, but divinely given. « Thine enemies. » The pagans. « The enemy. » The Jew, who is an enemy of God, while he defends the Father alone: because « he that honoureth not the Son, honoureth not « the Father, » or an enemy in his will.

« For I shall see. » Before the Jew, in spirit. « Thy heavens, » the apostles, I shall see present in their descendants; this well suits those of the first age. « The works of thy fingers. » Because they are perfected by the cooperation of the Trinity, which is signified here in the three fingers, as there: « Who weigheth the bulk of the earth with three fingers. » ((Isa. XL.)) And through them, « The moon and the stars which thou hast founded. » Not they.

« What is man. » ((Ibid.)) Secondly, he says that the nature of man, once corrupted, is exalted in Christ above all things. For before he had shown the omnipotence of the Godhead. By man, sinners; by the son of man, the spiritual. ((Ibid.)) Man, any vile person, of whom God is mindful in showing mercy, the Son of man, Christ as man: since through him thou visitest him, when the Word was made flesh, in which the physician came to the sick. « Or the son. » ((AUG.)) The disjunction hints that there is a distance between man and the son of man. Every son of man is man, but not conversely, as Adam. Every man therefore, who bears the image of the earthly: the Son of man, who is heavenly, and deservedly a new man, son of man: because the new is made out of the old by a certain change. ((AUG.)) Why, leaving the higher things, does he speak of these lowest ones? But the sheep, etc., *as far as* who by the seed of the word of God make the hearts of men to bear fruit.

« Moreover the cattle also. » He notes therefore that the wicked also are subject to Christ, which seems less: for these carnal men dwell in the breadth of the plain, that is, in the amplitude of pleasures, not in the mountains of virtues. « The cattle of the field. » ((Ibid.)) Who live in the flesh, where they climb nothing steep: but the broad way, to which they cling, is that which leads to destruction: whence also Abel is slain in the field.

« The birds, » the proud: of whom, « They have set their mouth against heaven ((Psal. LXXII)). » Whose head says: « I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High ((Isa. XIV)). « The fishes of the sea that walk through the paths of the sea, » the curious. These three, the pleasure of the flesh, pride, curiosity, include all vices, which are the concupiscence of the flesh, the ambition of the world, that is, pride, the concupiscence of the eyes, since through the eyes curiosity chiefly prevails.

notes.text: But when the fulness of the time — Appointed by the Father, ver. 2. Was come, God sent forth - From his own bosom. His Son, miraculously made of the substance of a woman - A virgin, without the concurrence of a man. Made under the law - Both under the precept, and under the curse, of it.
To redeem those under the law — From the curse of it, and from that low, servile state. That we - Jews who believe. Might receive the adoption - All the privileges of adult sons.

And because ye — Gentiles who believe, are also thus made his adult sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts likewise, crying, Abba, Father - Enabling you to call upon God both with the confidence, and the tempers, of dutiful children. The Hebrew and Greek word are joined together, to express the joint cry of the Jews and gentiles.

Wherefore thou — Who believest in Christ. Art no more a servant - Like those who are under the law. But a son - Of mature age. And if a son, then an heir of all the promises, and of the all- sufficient God himself.

glossa.text:
*The fulness of time came.* That is, after that whole space was fulfilled through which the law was to endure, then God sent, etc. *The fulness of time.* He knew when he ought to come, or even to suffer, etc. For there is no hour of his, or of ours, save his will. Yet before it a long series of heralds had to be sent ahead.

*God sent his Son.* Whence, *I went forth from the Father, and came into this world ((Joan. XVI))*. And yet of him John the Evangelist says: *He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not ((Ibid. I))*. Then he joins: *He came unto his own.* Thither therefore was he sent, where he was. Whence also the Prophet says that: *I fill heaven and earth ((Jer. XXIII))* . It is to be asked therefore how that sending is to be understood. If therefore we think soberly of the Son of God the things that are worthy, we ought to understand him to have been sent for this reason, because out of that incomprehensible and unutterable secret of the deep majesty the Word of God gave himself to be comprehended by our minds, not only when he emptied himself, but also when he dwelt among us. *Of a woman.* The usage of the Hebrew tongue calls women not those that are corrupted, but females. *Made under the law.* That he might appear circumcised, as a son of Abraham having the sign of him to whom he had been promised; in whom circumcision was fulfilled: and so let the sign now cease. For Abraham believed that he should have a son, in whom all nations should be blessed: which we believe to be already done.

*That the adoption.* That is, that we might be partakers of the divine glory. For as he himself partakes by nature, so he adopts us unto the seeing of it. For hence we receive adoption, that that only Son of God did not disdain a partaking of our nature, made of a woman, that he might not only be the only-begotten, but might also be made the first-born among many brethren. But he says adoption, that we may distinctly understand the only Son of God.

*God sent.* For that we might be proved to have been adopted by God unto sons, he gave us his Spirit who should show the sign of the Father toward the sons, that, because we should not dare to say this by our infirmity and unworthiness, he might prompt us to dare to say it. *The Spirit of the Son.* Note that the Spirit is the Son's also. And note here also the Trinity. ((AUG.)) If perchance anyone should ask whether the Spirit proceeds from the Son, etc., *as far as* he has from him, that from him also the Holy Spirit should proceed.

*Crying.* It is to be noted that in the Scriptures a cry is understood not as the sending forth of a great voice, but as the greatness of knowledge and of doctrines.

*Abba father.* Elegantly he set down two words signifying the same thing, on account of the whole people which out of Jews and Gentiles has been called into the unity of faith, that the word of the Hebrews might pertain to the Hebrews, the Greek to the Gentiles. But the same signification of each word pertains to the unity of the same faith and Spirit.

*Who by nature are not,* etc. He shows that the nature of the true God is one, namely of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But what is it to be God by nature, save to be true God? Whence elsewhere the Apostle: *You are converted to serve the living and true God ((I Petr. II))* .

notes.text: For all the things that they had heard — From Mary; as it was told them - By the angels.

To circumcise the child — That he might visibly be made under the law by a sacred rite, which obliged him to keep the whole law; as also that he might be owned to be the seed of Abraham, and might put an honour on the solemn dedication of children to God.

glossa.text: *And they came with haste. ((BEDA.))* The presence of Christ is not to be sought with sloth, etc., *as far as* they will find him as it were in a manger.
*And seeing.* It is the vision or knowledge of God, and this alone is the life of men, that they should know the true Father, and that Jesus Christ, whom he sent, is one God.

*They wondered.* They wonder both at the mystery of the incarnation and at so great a testimony of shepherds, who did not know how to feign what they had heard, but with a simple eloquence proclaimed true things. But the Lord appointed not orators but fishermen to preach the Gospel. So too in the Old Testament he ordained shepherds as the messengers of his dispensation. Therefore the testimony of the shepherds is not to be lightly esteemed.

*And returning,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Thus spiritual shepherds, while others sleep, are borne up by contemplating heavenly things, etc., *as far as* when they say: *Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.*

registers.label: Spare
lines: The Lord bless you and keep you.
How majestic is your name in all the earth.
On the eighth day he was named Jesus: God saves.
How majestic is your name in all the earth.
Because we are children, God has sent the Spirit into our hearts.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Speak it slowly — the name given before he was born, the name that means God saves.
How majestic is your name in all the earth!
The same God who set the moon and stars has bent down to name a child.
How majestic is your name in all the earth!
And by that name we are no longer slaves but daughters and sons.
How majestic is your name in all the earth!
So we cry out the name written on our hearts: Abba, Father.
How majestic is your name in all the earth!

How majestic is your name in all the earth! Amen.
